report:
The evidence actually contradicts the assumption that arthroscopy helps knee osteoarthritis — the answer is essentially "no," not "yes."

**Report**

High-quality trials and systematic reviews consistently show arthroscopic surgery (debridement, lavage, partial meniscectomy) provides little or no meaningful benefit for knee osteoarthritis:

- Moseley et al.'s landmark placebo-controlled RCT (NEJM, 2002) found arthroscopic debridement or lavage produced outcomes no better than sham surgery for pain or function in knee OA (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa013259).
- Kirkley et al.'s RCT (NEJM, 2008) compared arthroscopic surgery plus optimized medical/physical therapy to medical therapy alone in moderate-to-severe knee OA and found no added benefit from surgery (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0708333).
- A 2015 BMJ systematic review/meta-analysis of arthroscopic knee surgery for degenerative disease (including OA and meniscal tears) found only small, short-term pain improvements that did not meet minimal clinically important thresholds, alongside surgical harms, concluding the evidence does not support the practice (https://www.bmj.com/content/350/bmj.h2747).
- Cochrane's summary of arthroscopic debridement trials similarly concludes it "probably does not improve pain or function" compared with placebo (https://www.cochrane.org/evidence/CD005118_arthroscopic-debridement-osteoarthritis-knee).
- A 2024 systematic review/meta-analysis (BMC Musculoskeletal Disorders) likewise concluded arthroscopic surgery is not superior to conservative treatment for knee OA.

Based on this convergent body of RCTs and meta-analyses, current clinical guidelines (e.g., BMJ Rapid Recommendations) strongly advise against arthroscopy for degenerative knee disease/osteoarthritis, including when accompanied by meniscal tears, except in select cases with mechanical locking or other specific indications.

**Conclusion:** The evidence does not support the belief that arthroscopy helps knee osteoarthritis. Multiple placebo-controlled and comparative trials show no clinically meaningful benefit over sham surgery or conservative care, and guidelines now recommend against routine use.
